questions.problem:
$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}{e}^{x+2}, & x\in [-2,0) \\ 1, & x\in [0,2)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the function $F(x)$ shown above. Find the value to which the Fourier series of the $4$-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ converges when $x=-2.$

The Fourier series converges to {{field-1}} when $x=-2.$
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose that $f(x)$ is a $2L$-periodic piecewise smooth function with the corresponding Fourier series

$$
S(x)=\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x).
$$

Then, the series converges for all $x\in R.$

- If $f(x)$ is continuous at $x,$ then the series converges to the value of the function at this point:

$$
S(x)=f(x)
$$

- If $f(x)$ has a jump discontinuity at $x,$ then the series converges to the midpoint between the values of left- and right-sided limits of the function at this point:

$$
S(x)=\frac{{f}^{-}(x)+{f}^{+}(x)}{2}
$$

where ${f}^{-}(x)$ and ${f}^{+}(x)$ are the left- and right-sided limits of the function at this point, respectively.

Notice that the $4$-periodic extension $f(x)$ of our function $F(x)$ is not continuous at $x=-2.$ The one-sided limits at this point are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-}(-2) & ={lim}_{x\to -{2}^{-}}f(x)=1 \\ {f}^{+}(-2) & ={lim}_{x\to -{2}^{+}}f(x)={e}^{-2+2}=1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, the Fourier series of $f(x)$ converges to 

$$
\frac{{f}^{-}(-2)+{f}^{+}(-2)}{2}=\frac{1+1}{2}=1.
$$

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-26, & x\in [-5,0) \\ -3x, & x\in [0,5)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the function $F(x)$ shown above. Find the value to which the Fourier series of the $10$-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ converges when $x=5.$

The Fourier series converges to {{field-1}} when $x=5.$
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose that $f(x)$ is a $2L$-periodic piecewise smooth function with the corresponding Fourier series

$$
S(x)=\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x).
$$

Then, the series converges for all $x\in R.$

- If $f(x)$ is continuous at $x,$ then the series converges to the value of the function at this point:

$$
S(x)=f(x)
$$

- If $f(x)$ has a jump discontinuity at $x,$ then the series converges to the midpoint between the values of left- and right-sided limits of the function at this point:

$$
S(x)=\frac{{f}^{-}(x)+{f}^{+}(x)}{2}
$$

where ${f}^{-}(x)$ and ${f}^{+}(x)$ are the left- and right-sided limits of the function at this point, respectively.

Notice that the $10$-periodic extension $f(x)$ of our function $F(x)$ is not continuous at $x=5.$ The one-sided limits at this point are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-}(5) & ={lim}_{x\to {5}^{-}}f(x)=-3(5)=-15 \\ {f}^{+}(5) & ={lim}_{x\to {5}^{+}}f(x)={5}^{2}-26=-1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, the Fourier series of $f(x)$ converges to 

$$
\frac{{f}^{-}(5)+{f}^{+}(5)}{2}=\frac{-15+(-1)}{2}=-8.
$$

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡x, & x\in [-\frac{\pi }{2},0] \\ {e}^{x}, & x\in (0,\frac{\pi }{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the function $F(x)$ shown above. Find the value to which the Fourier series of the $\pi $-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ is converging when $x=-\frac{\pi }{3}.$

The Fourier series converges to {{field-1}} when $x=-\frac{\pi }{3}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose that $f(x)$ is a $2L$-periodic piecewise smooth function with the corresponding Fourier series

$$
S(x)=\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{L}x).
$$

Then, the series converges for all $x\in R.$

- If $f(x)$ is continuous at $x,$ then the series converges to the value of the function at this point:

$$
S(x)=f(x)
$$

- If $f(x)$ has a jump discontinuity at $x,$ then the series converges to the midpoint between the values of left- and right-sided limits of the function at this point:

$$
S(x)=\frac{{f}^{-}(x)+{f}^{+}(x)}{2}
$$

where ${f}^{-}(x)$ and ${f}^{+}(x)$ are the left- and right-sided limits of the function at this point, respectively.

Notice that the $\pi $-periodic extension $f(x)$ of our function $F(x)$ is continuous at $x=-\frac{\pi }{3}.$ 

Therefore, the Fourier series of $f(x)$ converges to 

$$
f\,(-\frac{\pi }{3})=cos\,(-\frac{\pi }{3})=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

$$

Select the correct options in the reasoning below.

At $x=0,$ we have

\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\cdot 0)={{field-1}}.

at $x=0,$ the corresponding Fourier series converges to

questions.worked_solution:
First, we rewrite our Fourier series as

$$
f(x)∼\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{3}+4{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(nx).
$$

Now, notice that at $x=0,$ we have

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\cdot 0)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)=1.
$$

Since $f(x)$ is $\text{continuous}$ at $x=0,$ the corresponding Fourier series converges to 

$$
f(0)=0.
$$

 

Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0) & =\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{3}+4{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\cdot 0) \\ 0 & =\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{3}+4{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}}\cdot 1 \\ -\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{3} & =4{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}} \\ {\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}} & =-\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{12} \\ {\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{2}} & =\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}4, & x\in [-\pi ,0] \\ -2, & x\in (0,\pi )\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the function $F(x)$ shown above. The Fourier series of the $2\pi $-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ is given by

$$
f(x)∼1-{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{12}{\pi (2n-1)}sin\,((2n-1)x).
$$

Select the correct options in the reasoning below.

At $x=\frac{\pi }{2},$ we have

$$
sin\,((2n-1)\cdot \frac{\pi }{2})={{field-1}}.
$$

Since $f(x)$ is 
{{field-2}}
at $x=\frac{\pi }{2},$ the corresponding Fourier series converges to 

$$
f(\frac{\pi }{2})={{field-3}}.
$$

Therefore, we have 

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{2n-1}={{field-4}}.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we rewrite our Fourier series as

$$
f(x)∼1-\frac{12}{\pi }{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{2n-1}\cdot sin\,((2n-1)x).
$$

Now, notice that at $x=\frac{\pi }{2},$ we have

$$
sin\,((2n-1)\cdot \frac{\pi }{2})=sin\,(-\frac{\pi }{2}+n\pi )=(-1)^{n+1}.
$$

Since $f(x)$ is $\text{continuous}$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{2},$ the corresponding Fourier series converges to 

$$
f(\frac{\pi }{2})=-2.
$$

 

Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =1-\frac{12}{\pi }{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{2n-1}\cdot sin\,((2n-1)\cdot \frac{\pi }{2}) \\ -2 & =1-\frac{12}{\pi }{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{2n-1}\cdot (-1)^{n+1} \\ -3 & =-\frac{12}{\pi }{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{2n-1} \\ {\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{2n-1} & =\frac{\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$
